# **Monthly precious metal report** 

_Gold, silver, platinum and palladium June 2012_ 

#### **David Jollie** 

**david.jollie@mitprecious.com Tel: +44 20 7489 6767** 

**19 July 2012** 

#### **New York:** 

-  In the run up to the Northern hemisphere summer months, price action was unexciting in the precious metals sector. The main drivers were still macroeconomic ones with precious metal traders finding a knowledge of Chinese economic conditions, the European political system and the deliberations of the US Federal Reserve over unconventional monetary policy more useful than any specific knowledge on the precious metal sector itself. 

-  Investor sentiment has turned progressively less bullish on the major precious metals over recent months. Speculative positioning has fallen in all four metals and ETF buying has been uninspiring. QE3 remains the real focus of the market. 

-  Resource nationalism remains a major issue for the mining sector. Although the South African Government has shown less interest in nationalisation of its mining industry than some had feared, developments in Argentina, Bolivia, Kyrgyzstan and Mongolia reinforce the impression that this topic is one to keep a close eye on. 

 In the platinum group metals, we have now started to see a wider supply-side response to a sustained period of low prices. Although only a few announcements over mothballing of active mining operations have been made, capital expenditure is being cut. This should provide some support not only for platinum prices but also for palladium and rhodium. In the longer term, if we believe in higher demand to come (which we do), this current underinvestment could lead to greater cyclicality in prices.

2 **Mitsui Global Precious Metals | Monthly Precious Metal Report** **19 July 2012** ## **Overview** Throughout June, the market focused on macroeconomic issues almost to the exclusion of all fundamental news. Our preferred measure of this myopia (short-sightedness) over fundamentals is a comparison between wheat and palladium prices. Other than their status as commodities, we feel that there is little in common between these two commodities. Indeed economics 101 suggests that US weather would affect wheat demand while Chinese automotive sales should have an influence on palladium prices. So, if both assets are trading in tandem, this would suggest that either Chinese automotive sales and US weather are correlated or that commodity-specific fundamentals are not in play. As can be seen from the graph below, palladium and wheat prices have moved closely together in recent months (until recently, see the palladium section below on page 22....), leading us to believe that the market’s concerns are wider in nature. **_Figure 1_** _: When prices of commodities move in concert, it suggests that the market is not focusing on fundamentals._ It should come as no surprise that these issues of concern are related to the outlook for the global economy, the fluid situation in Europe and the prospects of further quantitative easing (QE3) in the USA. Looking at the global economy, our current expectations are still for a low level of growth this year. However, even excluding the Eurozone economy, there are clear concerns over the health of the US recovery and over Chinese growth. Purchasing Manager Index data provides a simple forward-looking measure of economic activity. Although it shows both of these economies still growing (with PMI figures above 50 until recently), the rate of growth is slowing in each. The European economy is not in a happy place at the moment. Although we continue to believe that Greece and the other peripheral nations can rema

in within the Euro, it is no longer entirely clear that they will remain inside the single currency. Until there is some clarity on this issue, the European economy is likely to be stuck in neutral or in reverse and to act as a drag on global economic growth. Chinese growth is certainly substantially slower than it was in 2010 but that pace of expansion never seemed entirely sustainable. A weak European economy is hurting Chinese exporters and some early signs of excess investment in housing and infrastructure will also dent growth. However, with the governing politburo set to change later this year, and plenty of financial firepower available, we expect to see the Chinese Government embarking on a new stimulus programme to support economic activity in the coming months. **_Figure 4_** _: The US economy is growing more strongly than many others but is facing headwinds._ 4 **Mitsui Global Precious Metals | Monthly Precious Metal Report** **19 July 2012** A number of tax cuts are scheduled to expire later this year and cross-party agreement will have to be reached in order to extend them. Although discussions are likely to be fraught, we feel that a compromise will be reached and the US will not be thrown into recession over this issue. However, employment figures are disappointing and the recovery is rather fragile. A very slow European economy and comparatively sluggish growth in many emerging markets mean that the US economy is likely to struggle although a recession could well be avoided if the European situation does not deteriorate

too rapidly. The question this leads to is two-fold: is US growth strong enough to drive metal prices higher or is it weak enough to encourage further quantitative easing? We do not feel that US economic activity can lift prices alone so what about the prospects for QE? ### **The outlook for quantitative easing** It is important to note that the Federal Reserve has a multiple mandate: moderate long term interest rates, stable prices and maximum employment within the USA. We do not feel that the current situation within the USA justifies quantitative easing. However, with employment low compared to its pre-crisis levels, and the threat of further disruption from Europe affecting North America, we feel that there is growing justification for the launch of a third round of quantitative easing. In timing terms, the next FOMC meeting dates are at the start of August and in mid-September. Although the Fed is independent, launching QE3 close to the date of the Presidential election might be perceived as political and we think this is therefore unlikely. The most likely timing for QE is therefore during the third quarter of the year or in December, after the election has taken place. The effect of QE3, if and when it is launched, is likely to be positive for asset prices. And, on each occasion the Fed chooses not to launch QE3, commodity prices are likely to draw back to some extent. However, it is informative to look at what happened to commodity prices when QE2 was rumoured and then finally announced. QE2 was finally launched on the 3rd of November 2010 ( **B** on the graph below) after Ben Bernanke had hinted at it in late August ( **A** ). It ran until the start of June. Between the first two dates (A and B), silver firmed by 30 per cent even before QE2 was announced. In the following six months, it reached a new high ( **C** ) and fell back but still gained another 45 per cent ( **D** ) on its August-2011 levels. Recent price behaviour - sagging on each occasion when the Federal Reserve chooses not to announce or hint at the onset of QE3 - suggests that we are currently somewhere between A and B on this graph, with some of the impact of QE3 already built into the price. Although the impact of a third round of QE is likely to be less positive for asset prices than the first two were, there is still plenty of scope for higher prices if and when it is launched. From the start of the month to its end,

gold gained a few Dollars, moving from $1,560 in late May to $1,597 at the end of June, ending the run of four successive monthly declines in the price. There were, though, really only two price movements of interest: at the start of the month, terrible US non-farm employment figures in the USA sent the Euro higher and prompted hopes of US quantitative easing. Gold rallied from $1,550 to $1,630 that day before the market’s energy dissipated. 

European developments such as a proposed bail-out of ailing Spanish banks or the second Greek election, pushed the price one way or another but the next move came on the 20<sup>th</sup> . The FOMC decided to extend Operation Twist instead of launching a new programme of QE. The Dollar firmed and gold was sold off by disappointed investors. It found support at $1,560 the following day and at $1,550 on the 28<sup>th</sup> before seemingly positive news emerged from the latest European summit to push gold back close to $1,600 to end the month. Throughout this period, the market showed its lack of interest in anything other than the outlook for QE and the distant prospects of some (good or bad) resolution to the European debt crisis. 

However, the longer term price behaviour is perhaps more interesting. As of mid-July, the gold price had lost all of the ground it had gained in January and February and retreated to $1,565, almost exactly the level at which it started the year. Given the overt bullishness of the market at the start of this year, this dispiriting price performance has tested the resolve of many investors. In recent months, gold has been firmly in a downtrend, with even June’s relatively positive price performance almost entirely in keeping with a series of lower lows and lower highs. With the (Northern hemisphere) summer months approaching, further price weakness may be expected in the absence of any US-response to economic weakness. 



**_Figure 6_** _: It is hard even for the most bullish to maintain a constructive view on gold prices after a prolonged period of price declines._ 

The gold price has been stuck in this downtrend for almost a year now but, from a technical perspective, the price development seems to be in a continuation pattern: in other words, a simple retracement of the price from its highs does not indicate the end of an upwards trend in the price. However, investors with shorter term time horizons are unlikely to return to the market until something changes... 

It is, though, worth noting that in Euro terms, the price looks rather healthier. Although gold has not recorded a series of new Euro highs during 2012, the prices has certainly not weakened significantly. In recent weeks, gold has actually strengthened, showing the role that foreign exchange movements have played in the price. Until a credible plan to solve

**_Figure 7_** _: Gold does, though, look more attractive to European investors._ ### **Gold production** Some major gold projects have been in the news recently, reinforcing the theme of resource nationalism that we have previously seen and commented upon. As the examples below indicate, we are not too concerned yet over the impact of resource nationalism on the gold market but we are keeping this area under close observation. In Kyrgyzstan, Centerra Gold has operated the Kumtor mine since 1997. This single operation accounts for over ten per cent of the country’s economy. However, after recent allegations that the mine was causing environmental problems, the Kyrgyz parliament voted to review its operating license and to increase the nation’s ownership of the project (or increase the financial benefits accruing to the government from the project). In Mongolia, the huge Oyu Tolgoi operation (which is planned to produce in excess of 300,000 ounces of gold and 3 million ounces of silver per year) is currently being developed with plans to go into commercial production next year. With elections having recently taken place within Mongolia, there has been political pressure, as elsewhere, to subject foreign operations to enhanced regulatory oversight and potentially for ownership of this mine to be renegotiated (for which read, not in the favour of the mining company). It currently seems that cooler heads are winning the argument but the elections have increased the number of parliamentarians who advocate national ownership of mineral resources, adding further pressure to make changes. Recently, new regulations were introduced to limit foreign ownership of mineral deposits to 49 per cent without specific approval from Government. Oyu Tolgoi will make up a huge proportion of the national economy and more sensible politicians have noted that any action to change a deal that was itself only negotiated in 2009 would be hugely negative for investment in the country. Newmont’s Minas Conga operation in Peru is similarly under development. Capital costs are expected to be close to $5 billion and once the mine starts producing in late 2014 or early 2015, it is forecast to produce over 300,000 ounces of gold per year throughout the twenty year life of mine. Here, local activism has interrupted development with local unrest developing over environmental issues in particular. These have interrupted the construction process. When Ollanta Humala was elected as President

of Peru, there were concerns that the government might become more populist and that mining might become significantly more difficult. There are few signs of any such populism with the national Government taking a pragmatic view that the development of new mining operations and jobs should bring more economic benefits. Local environmental issues are problematic but the national Government seems keen for this mine to be developed.

### **Basel 3: the effect on gold** 

The Basel 3 rules, which are currently under discussion, aim to improve the banking sector’s ability to absorb external shocks. Although the proposed rules are numerous and widespread, the main impact on the gold market should be from changes to the amount and quality of capital held by a bank. Once they are finally agreed, these are scheduled for implementation between 2013 and the start of 2019. 

There are two issues of greatest relevance to the market: the liquidity coverage ratio (LCR) and the net stable funding ratio (NSFR) for the banking sector. 

The liquidity coverage ratio is designed to ensure that banks have sufficient levels of liquid assets that can be liquidated in order to avoid short term liquidity issues. This focuses on so-called high quality liquid assets (HQLA). Gold is currently omitted from the set of assts included in this set of HQLA. In our view, this makes little sense: gold is a highly liquid, widely traded asset which often behaves in a similar way to cash or to government bonds. It seems likely that it will be included in this list of qualified assets (although it is not clear whether this would apply to allocated or unallocated gold). This should make gold a more attractive asset for financial institutions to hold, resulting in stronger “demand”. These rules are set to be phased in by 2015 so, if gold does achieve this status, the impact should not be immediate. 

In the net stable funding ratio, the aim is to better match short term liabilities with short term funding. High liquidity assets are assigned a low required stable funding (RSF) factor, while longer term assets are given a higher RSF factor, which means that they have to be funded by longer term, stable funding. A more liquid asset is more attractive to own and the desire to hold gold would be increased by a lower RSF rating. Again, to us, gold is an attractive asset which should have a low RSF factor and it seems more than possible that gold will achieve this. These rules are set for implementation before 2017. 

It is indisputable that gold demand should benefit from a greater official appreciation of its value as a financial asset. There is no doubt that these new rules toughen the capital requirement regime affecting the banking sector and will require the holding of additional capital and of higher quality capital. How much gold benefits will depend on how a wide range of other assets are trea

ted in these rules and we do not feel that it is possible yet to estimate the impact on gold “demand” or gold prices. 

### **Gold in China and India** 

Gold buying interest in China continues to be very strong despite a degree of price softness. Price weakness is normally a negative for investors who prefer to buy into a rising price in the anticipation of near term “profits”. The World Gold Council has recently downgraded its expectations for overall demand from 1,000 tonnes this year to “only” 870 tonnes (which would still represent an increase in weight terms of 13 per cent compared to 2011). The key buying season will be in late September and the first half of October, around the Golden Week holidays. If prices show some strength during that period, demand could yet be above this new estimate. We will also be interested to see whether the loosening of credit availability within China leads to greater short term speculative interest in gold. We expect it to do so. 

Comments from the Bombay Bullion Association suggest that demand for gold within India should be stronger in the second half of the year than in the first half of year. However, their estimates are only that demand could rebound from 250 tonnes to 300 tonnes in that six month period. This annual demand would still be substantially below last year’s imports of just under 1,000 tonnes, demonstrating the drag that weak Indian demand is having on the gold market. 

What needs to happen to drive greater buying interest in gold within India? The recent tax

and duty increases have weighed on demand. Additionally, the jewellers’ strike hurt demand through the middle of H1. The fact that the jeweller’s strike has ended should mean that H2 volumes will be higher than H1 in any case. We feel that the major negative impact of the new import duty system was the initial disruption of its introduction rather than any additional impact on price sensitivity. Although the duty charged could be raised in the second half of the year in a continued effort to improve India’s balance of payments, we still expect it to have a less negative impact in the coming months. 

Of greater concern are the local gold price and the monsoon weather. The Rupee has weakened significantly since late last year, making gold much more expensive in local terms. Any fall in the domestic price of gold would be positive for gold investment and jewellery demand. If this is derived from a fall in the USD gold price, this should be negative for Chinese demand and the overall impact might be roughly neutral. A more positive change would be for the Rupee to show some strength: this might derive from increasing risk appetite or from a weaker US Dollar. There are some recent signs of stability in the Rupee’s exchange rate against the Dollar but it would be hopeful rather than scientific to assume already that this will lead to greater Ind

ian physical buying of gold. We have insufficient knowledge of meteorological conditions within India to comment in detail but reports suggest that rainfall has been below average and patchy, suggesting that gold demand could be weaker than last year. ### **Gold investment in June** Sales of gold coins by the US Mint were 60,000 ounces during June, almost exactly the same level as during June 2011. For the year-to-date, sales are 341,000 ounces, very substantially lower than the 576,000 ounces sold in the first half of 2011. ETF positions increased from an initial 69.8 million ounces to 70.5 million ounces as the Greek elections loomed. The buying slowed in the second half of the month, though, as a (relatively) proausterity Greek Government was actually elected. With five of the last six weeks having seen net ETF buying of gold, some positive momentum could now be developing amongst ETF investors. Interestingly, much of this buying was in Europe-based funds suggesting that it is being driven by risk aversion as much as by the prospect of price appreciation. COMEX “flows” were mixed throughout June. As we mentioned above, when the gold price moved on prospects of QE3, net long speculative positioning waxed and waned at the same time. At the start of the month, they increased by 3.4 million ounces in one week and at the end of the month they shrank by 2.6 million ounces. The market’s obsession with quantitative easing is plain to see. Throughout, net positioning remained low, at well below 20 million ounces. Throughout 2011, speculators were noticeably more positive about gold’s short term prospects. It is worth noting though, that margins are substantially higher than they were through the first half of 2011, suggesting that any future cut in initial and maintenance margins should be positive for gold prices. **_Figure 9_** _: The silver price continued to languish under $30 an ounce during June._ The silver price dropped both during June and throughout the second quarter of 2012, in sharp contrast to the move higher towards $50 an ounce which was seen one year earlier. In our view, the previous move was driven by good levels of industrial demand, momentum from a longer running move higher and a good level of investor interest (inspired partly by a second round of US quantitative easing). Indicators of these drivers inc

luded falling COMEX stocks, high physical premiums, rising ETF holdings and so on. In contrast, the market currently looks rather weak with COMEX stocks rising, premiums softer than a year earlier, uninspiring physical demand and a market that is still impatiently awaiting another round of quantitative easing by the US Federal Reserve. Although a strong gold price or a weak US Dollar could prompt a move to higher prices, there seems little fundamental reason to look for higher silver prices in the next few months. Price movements in June were driven by concerns over the economic outlook, weak physical demand and falling long investor interest, combined with a weak Euro in the second half of the month. In the first two weeks of June, silver firmed, rising from $27.70 to $28.70 around the fifteenth. Anyone watching without an eye on the currency markets might have believed that this was a sign of investors finally providing support for the silver price after its descent to sub-$30 levels. However, a surprising bout of Euro strength was the primary reason. Nonetheless, silver found support at the start of the month from poor US economic data which prompted the market to dream wistfully of further QE. A reduction in Chinese interest rates added more energy on the 6th of June but silver proved unable to breach $30, coming to a halt at $29.90 that day. Rumours of a possible bailout of the ailing Spanish banks firmed the Euro a touch, providing some support before the Federal Reserve revealed its views on quantitative easing. The decision to extend Operation Twist rather than print more money did not meet some of the market’s expectations. The Dollar firmed and silver retreated, finding little support. It fell to $26.20 or thereabouts on the 28th before more positive news from Europe over the first tentative moves towards a possible banking union. **_Figure 15_** _: Short COMEX interest is rising, suggesting that short term bearishness is growing..._ **_Figure 16_** _: ...while long interest has been declining for some time._ ### **Silver production** As with gold and the platinum group metals, resource nationalism is becoming more visible in the silver mining sector. In June and early July, South America was in focus. In Bolivia, the Government stepped in to revoke the mining license on a foreign-owned silver project (Malku Kota) following local unrest. President Evo Morales was quoted as saying “How can we be at odds with each other over an international company that comes to loot our natural resources?” Following the seizure of a zinc mine owned by Glencore, this action and rhetoric must be of some concern to the mining sector in this country.. Further South in Argentina, provincial legislation relating to the mineral sector is also a worry. **_Figure 19_** _: A weak platinum price confirms that the world economy is slowing._ The platinum price climbed during June, rising from $1,415 to a final $1,447 but the overall result was disappointing. In the middle of the month, platinum challenged the $1,500 level but having failed to break through that barrier convincingly in mid-June (and again in early July) it retreated back to closer to $1,400. In the process, it fixed at $1,402 towards the end of the month, its lowest level since the very start of the year. At the end of May, platinum sagged towards $1,400 on concerns over the health (or otherwise) of the Spanish banking sector. On the 1st of June, however, terrible US employment data came to the rescue: the market dared to dream of QE3 and a weak Dollar allowed platinum to race higher to $1,470 on the 6th and 7th . Platinum did slacken a little but an announcement that Aquarius and Anglo American Platinum were to mothball their Marikana mine injected a touch of energy into the price which continued higher. The relatively positive result from the Greek elections on the 18th helped the Euro to strengthen and platinum crawled back to $1,505 that day before risk aversion came back with a vengeance. Despite more hints of cuts from the platinum producers, the realisation that the FOMC was not about to unleash QE3 imminently saw the Euro weaken and platinum fall back to $1,422 on the 22nd and tumble further to $1,385 in the spot market on the 28th and 29th before recovering some ground to end the month above where it had started. ### **Reconciling low current prices and future bullishness** The low price of platinum is greatly at odds with the perception (and reality?) that the platinum price is currently unsustainably low. We tend to agree with the feeling

that platinum will trade higher in the medium term based on its attractiveness as a jewellery metal and utility as a catalyst and in other technical applications. As the world economy gradually improves and confidence finally starts to recover, demand should rise and prices are likely to rebound. However, in the short term, recent visits to industrial users of platinum (and the other precious metals) have confirmed that demand remains weak for two reasons: consumer and business spending has been negatively affected in Europe by a looming recession, and the possibility of a Euro break-up has caused great uncertainty. While there has been some buying interest from end consumers at low prices, this has therefore been limited in scale. Sales of platinum on the Shanghai Gold Exchange (a proxy for jewellery demand within China) are running at very similar levels to last year, suggesting that jewellery demand has not responded to lower prices and a discount to gold. However, our preferred measure, imports of platinum into Shenzhen, is more positive, suggesting that we can expect to see some growth in Chinese jewellery demand this year. This may not be enough to drive the price higher but should provide some support. Any further move towards loosening credit availability within China could encourage further stockbuilding by the jewellery industry which would be more price positive. 16 **Mitsui Global Precious Metals | Monthly Precious Metal Report** **19 July 2012** The first cuts in production by the mining sector (see below) in response to the low prices are also an important indicator of where the price might head in the long term. However, in the shorter term, investor sentiment is likely to be key in determining the price. We note that despite some ETF buying, the most obvious manifestation of investor interest has been the growth in short positioning on NYMEX in recent weeks. This has risen to record levels and, although the market is still net long, this is an indicator of investor concern over the potential for lower prices in the short term. With the Northern hemisphere summer already upon us (despite the inclement weather in London as this is written) good economic news is unlikely to emerge for some time and bearish sentiment could persist. In total, these mines _should_ produce more than 350,000 ounces of 4E metals per year when operating at steady state. In practice, the temporary closure should cut about 120,000 ounces of platinum production (and 60,000 ounces of palladium and 20,000 ounces of rhodium). So, are the cuts already announced enough to affect the market balance and price of platinum? We are relatively positive over platinum demand with the market likely to be close to balance this year. However, with the economic outlook highly uncertain, the desire for industrial or other consumers to buy forward future metal requirements is low. Stock levels at consumers are relatively high too. So, although we feel that these cuts could be enough to move this metal into deficit, it would take some time before any tightness is m

anifested in the physical platinum market. The more likely mechanism to provide support for the metal price is from the perception of determined action by the platinum producers to cut production. We feel that either one or both of Impala and Anglo American Platinum would need to cut their output in order to drive prices higher via this route. Could it start to recover?_ ### **Automotive demand** The automotive industry appears to be relatively healthy on a global basis, suggesting that uptake of palladium and rhodium is relatively strong. European passenger car sales fell by 6.8 per cent in the first six months of 2012 compared to H1 2011. There has also been a considerable amount of noise in the European press over the region’s excess manufacturing capacity and the possible responses, with PSA Peugeot-Citroen and Opel (GM’s continental European brand) the main focus of interest. However, even the European manufacturers are having a better time than their local sales alone would suggest: BMW has revealed that its six month global output was at record levels; PSA has expanded its output in Russia. We do, though, believe that the European market will remain weak for some time to come (a negative for platinum demand but also for palladium and rhodium). North American light duty vehicle sales are healthy, though. Production figures are much stronger in each of Canada, Mexico and the USA than they were a year ago. Car production is a fifth higher than it was in June 2011 while passenger truck output has risen by 16 per cent: clearly this is a very positive story for palladium demand. 23 **Mitsui Global Precious Metals | Monthly Precious Metal Report** **19 July 2012** However, inventory levels of unsold vehicles are rising and margins are falling. Truck inventories are higher than car inventories but both are higher than they were at the start of June 2012, or in July 2011. There are some clear risks that this recovery could slow in Q3 2012 but, for the moment, we remain relatively optimistic. Looking at China, the short term picture looks a little less positive, although we remain hopeful for the medium term. Car prices fell in June, a sign of weak consumer demand and excess inventory being held. Prices have fallen by almost two per cent in the last year: in the context of domestic inflation averaging four per cent, this is a significant improvement in affordability which should gradually help drive additional consumer demand but it is a short term sign of unconvincing demand. Overall, Chinese au

tomobile production climbed by 4.0 per cent from H1 2011 to 9.5 million units while sales grew by a little under 3 per cent. Expectations are currently that the second half of the year should be healthier than the first half of the year and that growth levels should be roughly five per cent this year. 

However, recent decisions to limits car sales in Guangzhou (one of China’s largest cities) from the start of July could trim another 200,000 units off annual sales figures this year (and prompted frenzied buying ahead of the restrictions being imposed). There are rumours that other major cities such as Shenzhen and Dalian could introduce local car registration restrictions in an effort to curb pollution and address traffic problems. We still feel that government stimulus efforts will outweigh these local restrictions on car ownership and that growth rates should creep higher but this is an area to monitor closely. 

### **Swiss imports of palladium** 

During May, Switzerland imported only 201kg of semi-fabricated palladium from Russia. In June, the equivalent figure was only 301kg of semi-fabricated metal. We believe that this is likely to be material from current production. 

For the first five months of the year, Swiss imports of palladium from Russia were 2.08 tonnes of raw metal (which could be sales of state stocks) and 1.4 tonnes of semi-fabricated material (which we do not believe is related to state stocks). Last year, unnamed sources suggested that only 4 to 4.5 tonnes of metal might be sold this year from the Russian state stocks of palladium and the first six months import figures fit very well with that comment. Assuming that these import figures remain low, this will provide support for the metal price. However, a lack of imports in any given month is unlikely to prompt a significant move to higher prices.

## **<mark>Ruthenium</mark>** 

Since there is little information on ruthenium which is publicly available, we rarely feature it in our regular reports. 

However, we recently noted a news story on this metal which we though worthy of reporting on. Tanaka has announced the opening of three new supply centres for ruthenium-based thin film precursors used in the manufacture of semiconductors. It has opened facilities in Taiwan, South Korea and the USA and will start supply from these locations in July 2012. It has apparently secured three years’ supply of ruthenium for this application. 

The specific use in question is in Dynamic Random Access Memory (or DRAM) technology which is set to move into mass production by the end of 2013, where ruthenium will be used as a base layer for copper plating. Although this is positive for ruthenium demand, this should not be a re-run of the introduction of ruthenium into hard disks several years ago: volumes will be lower and recycling can be carried out without returning the metal into its raw form,

with an associated reduction in metal inventories.
